essentials: EU ESG law is a set of connected rules rather than one law: companies **report** (CSRD, ESRS, Taxonomy), investors **disclose** (SFDR), supply chains are **checked** (CSDDD, EUDR, Forced Labour), carbon gets a **price** (EU ETS, CBAM), and **products and claims** are regulated (ESPR, PPWR, Batteries, ECGT).
A **regulation** applies directly in every Member State. A **directive** has to be written into national law first, so details and dates can differ from country to country.
Every act has up to three different dates: **entry into force**, **date of application** and, for directives, the **transposition deadline**. Mixing them up is the most common mistake in this field.
Since 2025 the direction of travel is **simplification**. The Omnibus packages narrowed who is covered and moved dates back; they did not abolish the framework.

sections.title: What ESG means in EU law
text: ESG stands for environmental, social and governance. It started as investor shorthand for the non-financial factors that affect a company's value and its effect on the world. EU law rarely uses the abbreviation itself. The CSRD speaks of **sustainability matters**: environmental, social and human-rights, and governance factors. The SFDR speaks of **sustainability factors** and **sustainability risks**.

The tracker marks each regulation with the pillars it mainly concerns. Many acts touch more than one: the CSDDD covers human rights (S) and the environment (E) and changes how boards oversee both (G).

sections.title: How an EU law is made
text: Almost every act in this tracker went through the **ordinary legislative procedure**. Knowing its steps tells you how far away a rule still is, and how likely it is to change.
steps: **Proposal.** Only the European Commission can propose legislation. The proposal gets a COM number, for example COM(2023) 166.

**Positions.** The European Parliament works through a lead committee (such as JURI, ECON or ENVI) and then votes in plenary. The Council, where the Member States sit, agrees a ‘general approach’ or negotiating mandate.
**Trilogues.** Parliament, Council and Commission negotiate a common text. The result is a ‘provisional agreement’.
**Adoption.** Parliament and Council each formally approve the agreed text. Only now is the content final.
**Publication and entry into force.** The act is published in the Official Journal and enters into force, typically on the twentieth day after publication.
**Application.** Obligations start on the date of application, which is often months or years later and may differ by company size.
after: The five stations on the tracker's rail follow this path: **Proposed**, **Negotiating**, **Adopted**, **In force**, **Applies**.

sections.title: Three levels of rules
text: The act adopted by Parliament and Council is only the first layer. Much of the practical detail sits below it.
points: **Level 1: the basic act.** The directive or regulation itself. It sets the obligations, the scope and the dates.

**Level 2: delegated and implementing acts.** Adopted by the Commission on the basis of Level 1. The ESRS, the Taxonomy's technical screening criteria and the SFDR templates are all Level 2. Parliament and Council can object to a delegated act during a scrutiny period, usually two months and extendable.
**Level 3: guidance.** FAQs, guidelines and Q&As from the Commission and the supervisory authorities. Not legally binding, but supervisors and auditors work with them, so they matter in practice.

sections.title: Who does what
points: **European Commission.** Proposes laws, adopts Level 2 acts, publishes guidance. Its departments are called DGs: FISMA handles reporting and sustainable finance, ENV and CLIMA the environmental and climate files, JUST consumer and company law, TAXUD the CBAM.

**European Parliament.** Co-legislator. Committees prepare its positions: JURI (legal affairs: CSRD, CSDDD), ECON (economic affairs: SFDR, Taxonomy), ENVI (environment: EUDR, ETS, CBAM, PPWR), EMPL (employment) and IMCO (internal market).
**Council of the EU.** Co-legislator, representing the governments of the Member States.
**EFRAG.** Private body that gives the Commission technical advice on the reporting standards.

**ESMA, EBA and EIOPA.** The European supervisory authorities for markets, banks and insurers. They draft technical standards for financial-sector rules and supervise ESG rating providers and green-bond reviewers.
**National competent authorities.** Enforce most rules on the ground: financial supervisors, customs, market surveillance and consumer authorities.

sections.title: Ideas that come up everywhere
points: **Double materiality.** A topic matters if the company has a significant impact on people or the environment, or if the topic creates significant financial risks or opportunities for the company. Either is enough.
**Value chain.** Many rules look beyond the company itself to suppliers and, sometimes, customers. How far they reach differs from act to act.

**Due diligence.** An ongoing process: identify risks of harm, prevent and mitigate them, track whether that works, communicate, and remedy harm that happened. It is an obligation to make appropriate efforts, not a guarantee of results.
**Scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions.** Direct emissions, emissions from purchased energy, and all other emissions in the value chain.
**Reach beyond the EU.** Rules attach to placing products on the EU market or generating turnover in the EU, so they also bind companies based elsewhere.
**Greenwashing.** Presenting a product, fund or company as more sustainable than it is. Much of the framework exists to make such claims checkable.

sections.title: From the Green Deal to the Omnibus
text: The **European Green Deal** of 2019 set the goal of climate neutrality by 2050, and between 2020 and 2024 most of the acts in this tracker were adopted. From late 2024 the political priority shifted to competitiveness and lower administrative burden.

The result is a series of **simplification packages**. Omnibus I, proposed in February 2025 and adopted in February 2026, cut the scope of the CSRD and the CSDDD to the largest companies. A ‘stop-the-clock’ directive postponed reporting waves in the meantime. Similar steps followed elsewhere: a mass threshold for CBAM, two postponements of the EUDR, later due diligence dates for batteries, and lighter Taxonomy reporting.

The pattern is consistent. Scope shrinks to the largest companies, dates move back, datapoints are cut. The core concepts, such as double materiality, risk-based due diligence and carbon pricing, stay in place.

mistakes.wrong: The act is in force, so companies have to comply now.
mistakes.right: Entry into force and application are different dates. The EUDR entered into force in June 2023 and applies from 30 December 2026.

mistakes.wrong: A directive means the same rules in every Member State.
mistakes.right: Directives are transposed into national law. Options, stricter national rules and late transposition create real differences.
It narrowed the scope to large companies and cut datapoints. Companies above the thresholds still report on a double-materiality basis.

mistakes.wrong: These rules only concern companies based in the EU.
mistakes.right: Many attach to EU market access or EU turnover and bind non-EU companies and, indirectly, their suppliers.

mistakes.wrong: A provisional agreement in trilogue is the final law.
mistakes.right: Both Parliament and Council still have to adopt it formally, and the text only counts once published in the Official Journal.

practice: When a headline reports a change, find the **type of act and its number** first. A regulation changes the rules directly; a directive starts a transposition period.
Place it on the rail: is it a **proposal**, an **agreed text**, or **published**? Only published text is certain.
Write down the **three dates**: entry into force, application, and transposition where relevant.
Check the **scope thresholds** before reading anything else. Most questions end there.
Ask whether **Level 2 acts or guidance** are still missing. Obligations often cannot be met in practice until they exist.
For directives, read the **national law** of each country where the company operates.

quiz.q: What is the key difference between an EU regulation and an EU directive?
options: A regulation applies directly in all Member States; a directive must be transposed into national law
A regulation is adopted by the Commission alone; a directive needs Parliament and Council
A regulation only binds companies; a directive only binds governments and public bodies
A directive applies immediately; a regulation needs a national implementing law
quiz.why: Regulations are directly applicable. Directives bind Member States as to the result and need national laws, which is why details can differ between countries.

quiz.q: An act ‘entered into force’ last month. What does that tell you about when companies must comply?
options: They must comply from that day
Nothing certain: the date of application can be much later
They must comply 20 days later
They must comply once guidance is published
quiz.why: Entry into force makes the act part of EU law. Obligations start on the date of application, which is set separately and is often staggered.

quiz.q: Who can formally propose new EU legislation?
options: The European Parliament
The Council of the EU
The European Commission
EFRAG
quiz.why: The Commission has the right of initiative. Parliament and Council then amend and adopt the proposal.

options: A vote of the three largest political groups in Parliament
Negotiations between Parliament, Council and Commission on a common text
A three-month scrutiny period for delegated acts
The three stages of transposition into national law
quiz.why: Trilogues are the informal negotiations in which the two co-legislators, with the Commission, agree a final text.

quiz.q: The ESRS and the Taxonomy's technical screening criteria are examples of what?
options: Level 1 basic acts
Level 2 acts adopted by the Commission
Level 3 guidance
National transposition measures
quiz.why: Both are delegated acts: binding detail adopted by the Commission on the basis of a Level 1 directive or regulation.

options: A topic must be both financially material and impact-material to be reported
A topic is material if it matters for the company's impact on people and the environment, or for its finances
Material topics must be reported twice, in the annual and the sustainability report
Materiality is assessed by the company and again by the auditor
quiz.why: The two perspectives are impact materiality and financial materiality. A topic that is material from either perspective has to be reported.

quiz.q: Which statement about the Omnibus I package is correct?
options: It repealed the CSRD and the CSDDD
It narrowed the scope of the CSRD and the CSDDD to larger companies and moved dates back
It turned both directives into directly applicable regulations
It extended reporting obligations to listed SMEs
quiz.why: Omnibus I (Directive (EU) 2026/470) raised the thresholds and reduced obligations. The frameworks themselves remain.

quiz.q: Parliament and Council have reached a provisional agreement on a file. Which stage of the tracker is it in?
options: Proposed
Negotiating
In force
Applies
quiz.why: A provisional agreement still needs formal adoption by both institutions. Until then the file counts as negotiating; ‘Adopted’ follows the formal votes.
